newsitem.title: FINLAND: INTERVIEW - Amer sees boost from share plan.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Amer sees boost from share plan.

text.p: A plan by Finnish sports goods group Amer to redeem shares carrying about one-tenth of votes and simplify shareholder structure should clear up historic problems that dogged its strategy, its chief executive said on Tuesday.

"This would mean we have solved a problem that the company has tried to solve for a very long time," Roger Talermo told Reuters, after Amer said it would redeem some stock and propose conversion of vote-heavy K-shares into listed A shares.

"If we can solve that -- as it looks today -- we will be even stronger to solve the business side," he said. Amer in January-April made a loss before extraordinaries and taxes of 49 million markka, against a 114 million loss in the year-ago period.

Talermo said the deal -- to redeem 275,000 K-shares which the Helsinki School of Economics and Business Administration had agreed to sell to British investor Lord Moyne -- would be financed from equity and have no earnings impact.
He said Amer has over 400 million markka in free share capital. "Financially it won't make any dent at all, in my opinion," he added.

On top of the redemption, Amer will propose to an August 26 extraordinary shareholders' meeting to simplify its ownership structure by converting K series shares to A stock, also increasing the A-holders' decision-making power.
Talermo said that unlike Amer's previous attempt at such conversion, in June, the company now had written undertakings from its remaining three main shareholders to support the plan.

That last effort was vetoed by an extraordinary meeting, when the four domestic Finnish institutions who controlled over 90 percent of votes through the K shares agreed to sell their stakes to the Briton.
That deal subsequently unwound after three of the four said Lord Moyne, or Jonathan Bryan Guinness, did not have enough guarantees.

"We have tried to eliminate the risk -- the possibility -- that again someone comes in between," Talermo said. "Nothing is sure before we have gone through the shareholders' meeting, but absolutely this is in that direction," he said.
"We would not try to go this way a second time if we did not think it will work," he added.
